a 5‐parameter model was developed to describe the time course of the decline and recovery of fibrinogen after a brown snake (Pseudonaja textilis) bite.
a systems model of coagulation can be simplified by a technique of lumping to a smaller model that describes a specific pharmacodynamic relationship.

the development and application of a systems coagulation model for describing the pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic relationship of brown snake venom–human fibrinogen.
developing a methodology to simplify systems biology models, with an emphasis on pharmacology and pharmacokinetics.
the simplification of a large systems biology model of the co-agulation network.

the model developed here can be used to predict the time course of recovery of fibrinogen after a brown snake envenomation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a systems biology model of coagulation can be reduced to a pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic model for describing a specific input– output process.

we have developed a systems coagulation model for brown snake venom, and we have reduced this model to a more tractable model that can be used to predict the time course of recovery of fibrinogen after a brown snake venom exposure.
the technique of proper lumpings can be used for the scale reduction of systems models and that the resulting models can be applied for the prediction of time courses of biomarkers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the systems pharmacology approach can be applied to the study of pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic data, and the resulting model can be simplified to a more tractable form.
the simplification of a complex systems model can be done while maintaining an appropriate level of mechanistic detail.
the complexity of systems pharmacology models can be reduced to a more manageable size while retaining a mechanistic relationship between the input and output processes.
